title: Dhaka says India is struggling to host Hasina and dismisses her December return
dek: 'You cannot simply throw out an unwanted guest,' a Bangladeshi minister said, a day after Delhi called her voluntary return separate from extradition. Dhaka has also written to India on the expiring Ganges treaty.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Bangladesh has dismissed Sheikh Hasina's plan to fly home in December and said India is beginning to feel the cost of hosting her, a day after Delhi said her voluntary return was a matter separate from Dhaka's extradition request. "You cannot simply throw out an unwanted guest," Humaiun Kobir, a state minister for foreign affairs, told reporters at the foreign ministry in Dhaka on Thursday, saying India "has also been feeling challenged and facing difficulties in this situation".

Mr Kobir said Hasina "falls under the criminal category and is subject to the extradition treaty", and brushed aside talk of a return on 16 December, Victory Day. "The only thing that'll arrive in December is winter," he said, according to reports, telling reporters they should buy jumpers. Dhaka has also written to India about the Ganges Water Treaty, which expires on 12 December, and is waiting for a reply, he said.

## Dhaka's reply to Delhi

Mr Kobir called Hasina "a psychopath" and "a terrorist" and said her presence in India was causing "unnecessary irritation". These are his claims; Hasina rejects the charges against her. He said Bangladesh's relationship was "with India's central government" and dismissed criticism from some politicians in West Bengal as the views of "crazy people". Asked about India's concern over violence against minorities in Bangladesh, he questioned the basis of the reports, asking whether an attack on minorities was "fake news or real news". On "Ganges water", he said: "We are doing whatever needs to be done from our side."

Three buses were set on fire in Dhaka on Thursday evening, two in the Pallabi area of Mirpur and one in Badda, by unidentified people, according to reports. No one was hurt. The officer in charge of Pallabi police station said police were working to identify those responsible; no group has claimed the attacks and no motive has been given. Police have blamed activists of the banned Awami League for several earlier arson attacks, which the party denies.

## India's position

On Wednesday India drew its clearest line yet. "The case of a citizen willing to return voluntarily to her country on a travel document is a matter separate from the extradition request," Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said at the ministry's briefing, adding that her return was a matter "between the former Prime Minister and the Bangladesh government". He said the extradition request, made under the interim government led by Muhammad Yunus, was "being examined in line with our established processes".

He also said India was "understandably" concerned at incidents of violence against minorities in Bangladesh and urged Dhaka to investigate them and "bring the perpetrators to justice". Earlier this month Hasina asked Bangladesh's High Commission, through a UK-based law firm, for a fresh passport, according to reports.

Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said on Wednesday that "a convicted fugitive" could return only through extradition, and that the Awami League would face strict legal action if it resorted to militancy or arson, according to reports.

## How the dispute began

On 24 November Hasina's spokesperson, Syed Mozammel Ali, said she would fly home on 16 December and asked the government to arrange her flight on the state carrier, Biman Bangladesh Airlines, noting that she had been flown to India on a Bangladeshi aircraft in August 2024. "It is deeply symbolic that she has chosen 16 December, our Victory Day," he said. It was the first time she had named a date since she fled Dhaka on 5 August 2024. Her claims could not be independently verified.

Dhaka rejected the request within hours. "She is not a regular commercial passenger," Mr Kobir said that morning. "She will have to return only in handcuffs or under strict surveillance." Abu Abdullah M Saleh, press secretary to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, said in an interview that she "has been convicted in a tribunal" and that the government had sought her extradition.

## Troops on the streets

The Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) said on Wednesday it had deployed 108 platoons in seven districts on the home ministry's instructions, 56 of them in Hasina's home district of Gopalganj, 18 in Dhaka and 18 in Gazipur, "to maintain law and order, ensure public safety and deal with any untoward situation", according to reports. A platoon has 30 to 40 personnel. The banned Awami League has called a nationwide "lockdown" for 29 and 30 November. In Gopalganj on 23 November at least 30 people were injured in clashes linked to its processions, according to reports.

## Background

Hasina ruled Bangladesh for 15 years until a student-led uprising forced her out in August 2024. The UN human rights office has said as many as 1,400 people may have been killed during the unrest. In November 2025 the International Crimes Tribunal in Dhaka sentenced her to death in absentia for crimes against humanity over the crackdown. She rejects the verdict and denies the charges, and a prosecutor has said she missed the deadline to appeal. Bangladesh allows presidential clemency, but she has not sought it.

The interim government led by Muhammad Yunus banned the Awami League's activities, and the party was barred from the February 2026 election. The Bangladesh Nationalist Party won it, and Tarique Rahman became prime minister. Jamaat-e-Islami is now the main opposition.

India has not said whether it will hand her over. In April the MEA said it was examining the extradition request and wanted to "engage constructively with the new government", and on Wednesday it repeated that the request was being examined.

## Why it matters for India and Bengal

Whatever Hasina does on 16 December, India is in the middle. Allowing her to fly to Dhaka would look to Bangladesh's government like India letting a convicted fugitive stage a political return; stopping her, or keeping her indefinitely, keeps the extradition dispute alive at a time when Delhi has said repeatedly that it wants a constructive relationship with the new government in Dhaka.

The dispute also lands on West Bengal's doorstep. On 22 November four senior Awami League leaders living in India visited the Petrapole land port in North 24 Parganas, Bangladesh's busiest trade crossing with India, and at the tribunal in Dhaka on 24 November reporters asked whether the government had failed by letting fugitives reach border areas such as Petrapole and Agartala. Any unrest around 16 December could affect the 2,217-km Bengal stretch of the border, cross-border trade and the movement of people.

It comes as other files between the two countries are open. The 1996 Ganges Water Treaty, which governs how the river's dry-season flow at Farakka is shared, expires on 12 December, and no date has been set for renewal talks.

## What happens next

- 29-30 November: the Awami League's called "lockdown" across Bangladesh.
- 12 December: the Ganges Water Treaty expires.
- 16 December: Hasina's stated return date, Victory Day in Bangladesh.

Whether Hasina can travel at all depends on documents Dhaka has so far refused to issue; India has now said publicly that this is a matter for her and the Bangladeshi government.
